hook_text: A hillside can move slower than your fingernails grow — or faster than a car on the N3. Same force.
clip_script: Every slope on earth is holding a tug-of-war. Gravity pulls everything downhill; friction, particle grip and plant roots hold it all up. Mass movement is the moment the rope changes hands — and it comes in six gears. Gear one: soil creep. The whole hillside skin slides slower than fingernails grow. You never see it move, only its paperwork — fence posts leaning drunk, tree trunks curved like bananas because the trees keep growing upright while their feet slip. Gear two: solifluction — cold porridge oozing over frozen ground in the high Drakensberg. Gear three: the landslide — a slab of hillside letting go all at once, like a bakkie sliding off a tow truck's flatbed. Gear four: the slump — the slide with a twist, rotating down a spoon-shaped surface, leaving a crescent bite above and a block tilted backwards below. Gear five: rock fall — no sliding, just free-fall, which is why mountain passes hang steel nets over the road. Gear six, the killer: the mud flow. Soak soil past every limit and it stops being ground — a river of porridge and boulders doing highway speeds, then setting like concrete around whatever it caught. The match-fixer in every gear is water: damp glues a sandcastle, a bucketful destroys it. That is why the slope that stood for fifty dry years fails in one soaked night — and why Durban's hills gave way in April 2022, when months of rain fell in a single day.
visual_style: A gear dial clicking from one to six, each gear cutting to its movement — creeping fence posts, oozing lobes, a sliding slab, a rotating slump block, a dropping boulder into a net, a racing mud flow — with a rain gauge filling ominously in the corner.
mood: Rising tension through the gears, sober and real at the close.
pacing: Slow first gear, each gear faster than the last, hard stop on the 2022 rain fact.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to read a hillside before the rain comes.
